intro.html: Written for a software engineer with no biology background. Ordered so each word only uses words defined above it. Read top to bottom the first time.
How an entry is written. One definition line and two optional italic lines under it:

• **term** — what it means. The definition, written for someone who has read only the entries above this one.
  • *Example: one concrete value.* A real value from the work or the published dataset schema, never an invented measurement.
  • *Context: where it is used · source: path/to/owner.md · related: term, other · see: [label](file.md) · first seen 2026-10-05* The metadata. Segments are separated by · (or ; before a key); every segment is optional. source: names the one repo-relative file that owns the term, related: the entries this one leans on, see: a figure, file or page worth opening. first seen is normally left out — app/tools/gen-dictionary.mjs derives it from git, taking the author date of the earliest commit that added the term's bold marker to this file, and you only write it by hand for a term that existed in the work before it reached this page.
The Learn page renders those as the definition, the example beneath it, and a quiet metadata footer carrying the date, the source, the related entries as links, and the exhibits.

Nothing in this repository has been measured against the challenge dataset. The files are not downloaded. Every concrete value quoted below is either (a) a published schema value the organisers supplied, owned by challenge.md, (b) a fact about this repository's own code, or (c) arithmetic that is explicitly labelled as arithmetic. A claim taken from the literature is written as a literature claim with a to verify flag, never as a settled fact.

Diagrams: mermaid blocks render automatically on GitHub, in VS Code with the Markdown preview, and in the app. Colour code used everywhere: green = good / safe / the goal, red = broken / dangerous / lost points, yellow = a decision point, blue = neutral machinery, purple = the raw input. Every diagram is followed by a > **Legend** line decoding its own colours and symbols, so you never have to guess what a shape means. Every diagram here is a Mermaid block, so the source is the picture and there is no binary asset to keep in step.

chapters.title: Proteins — the alphabet everything is written in

blocks.html: Start here. A protein is, for our purposes, a string over a 20-letter alphabet that folds into a shape. Both halves matter: the string is the input we are given, the shape is what decides what the protein touches.
one letter of the protein alphabet. There are 20 standard ones, each a small molecule with a common part (the same in all 20) and a distinguishing part.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: glutamine, written Q; valine, written V; leucine, written L.
blocks.context: the alphabet every sequence in this challenge is written over
blocks.source: standard protein biochemistry, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: the single uppercase character naming an amino acid. The 20 letters are ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY. B, J, O, U, X and Z are not standard residues; X conventionally means "unknown" and must be handled, not assumed absent.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the opening of the published ONU1 sequence reads MAQVQLQESGGGLVQAGG… — M, A, Q, V, Q, L, Q, E, S, G, G, G, …
blocks.context: the encoding of the sequence column

blocks.html: one amino acid once it is joined into a chain. The word you will see everywhere in this challenge: "interface residue", "per-residue prediction". A free amino acid is an amino acid; the same thing at position 57 of a chain is residue 57.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: residue 1 of the published ONU1 sequence is M (methionine).
blocks.context: the unit Track A predicts over — one probability per residue

blocks.html: the chemical link that joins one residue to the next, always in the same direction. It is why a protein is a sequence and not a set: the chain has a start (the N-terminus) and an end (the C-terminus), and by convention a sequence is always written N-terminus first, left to right.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: MAQ… means methionine is at the N-terminus, not the C-terminus.
blocks.context: why position indices are meaningful and stable
blocks.source: standard protein biochemistry, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: a chain of residues joined by peptide bonds, which folds into a specific three-dimensional shape and does a job. In software terms: a string that compiles itself into a machine.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: HER2 and a VHH nanobody are both proteins; this challenge is about how one touches the other.
blocks.context: the only kind of object in this challenge

blocks.html: one continuous protein molecule. A complex can contain several chains; each gets an identifier in a structure file. A VHH is one chain; a normal antibody is four.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: in this repository's record type the two chains are named binder and target.
blocks.context: the named halves of a SequenceRecord

blocks.html: the chain written out as a string of one-letter codes. Also called the primary structure. This is the entire input both tracks of the challenge are given.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the sequence column of AVIDa-hHER2.csv holds one of these per row.
blocks.context: the model input for both tracks — no structure is supplied

blocks.html: where a residue sits in the sequence. Biology counts from 1, not 0. Any code that indexes a sequence has an off-by-one waiting in it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "residue 1" is the first character of the string, i.e. sequence[0] in Python.
blocks.context: the row key of every per-residue prediction file

blocks.html: the universal plain-text format for sequences: a > header line, then the sequence on the following lines. Think of it as the .txt of molecular biology — no types, no schema, widely abused.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: >ONU1 on one line, then the amino-acid string on the next.
blocks.context: what almost every external model takes as input
blocks.source: standard sequence file format, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: the four-letter code (A, C, G, T) that cells store instructions in. It matters here for exactly one reason: the dataset was produced by sequencing DNA, so the amino-acid strings we analyse were read out as DNA first and translated.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the NGS_read_count_table.csv file counts DNA reads, not protein molecules.
blocks.context: why the dataset is a count table and not a list of measured affinities

blocks.html: three consecutive DNA letters, which name one amino acid. 64 codons map onto 20 amino acids plus a STOP signal, so the mapping is many-to-one and lossy in that direction.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ATG codes for methionine and also serves as the start signal.
blocks.context: the step between the sequencer's output and the protein string we model
blocks.source: standard genetic code, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: turning a DNA string into a protein string, three letters at a time. Pure function, no state: same DNA in, same protein out.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ATG GCT TCA TAA translates to Met-Ala-Ser then STOP.
blocks.context: how the sequenced library becomes the sequence column
blocks.source: standard genetic code, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: the part of a residue that differs between the 20 amino acids. It is the part that sticks out of the chain and does the touching, so almost everything about binding is side-chain chemistry.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: valine's side chain is small and greasy; glutamine's is polar and can form hydrogen bonds.
blocks.context: why interface prediction is not just geometry
blocks.source: standard protein biochemistry, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: the repeating part of the chain that is identical in every residue: the atoms the peptide bonds run through. The backbone carries the fold; the side chains decorate it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the CAPRI metric i-RMSDbb measures only backbone atoms — "bb" is backbone.
blocks.context: the atom subset several structure metrics restrict themselves to

blocks.html: a residue whose side chain avoids water. These tend to end up buried in the protein's core, or at a binding interface, which is itself shielded from water.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: valine V, leucine L, isoleucine I, phenylalanine F, tryptophan W.
blocks.context: one of the cheapest per-residue features available from sequence alone

blocks.html: a residue whose side chain is comfortable in water and can form hydrogen bonds.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: serine S, threonine T, asparagine N, glutamine Q, tyrosine Y.
blocks.context: the other half of the simplest sequence-only feature set

blocks.html: a polar residue carrying a positive or negative electrical charge. Opposite charges across an interface attract; like charges repel, so charge complementarity is a classic interface signal.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: positive — lysine K, arginine R; negative — aspartate D, glutamate E.
blocks.context: an interface feature that works across the two chains, not within one

blocks.html: the small repeating shapes the backbone falls into locally, before the whole chain folds. Three classes cover almost everything: helix, strand, and everything else.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a VHH is mostly beta strands joined by loops.
blocks.context: a standard intermediate feature — predictable from sequence alone with good accuracy

blocks.html: a corkscrew of backbone, roughly 3.6 residues per turn. Written H in most annotations.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: in a helix, residues i and i+4 sit on the same face.
blocks.context: one of the three secondary-structure classes

blocks.html: a stretched-out run of backbone. Several strands lie side by side to form a beta sheet. Written E in most annotations (for "extended").
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the immunoglobulin fold that a VHH adopts is a sandwich of two beta sheets.
blocks.context: the dominant secondary structure in antibody domains

blocks.html: the irregular connector between helices and strands. Loops are where a protein's individuality lives: they vary in length and sequence far more than the structured parts.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the three CDR loops of a VHH are loops in exactly this sense.
blocks.context: why "the binding site is in the loops" is a usable prior

blocks.html: the full three-dimensional shape of one folded chain: where every atom is. This is what Track B has to predict and Track A has to reason about without being given.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a VHH's tertiary structure is a compact barrel about 4 nanometres across.
blocks.context: the thing neither track is given as input

blocks.html: the recognisable family of tertiary structure a protein belongs to. Different sequences can share a fold; think interface, not implementation.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: every antibody variable domain, including every VHH, has the immunoglobulin fold.
blocks.context: why a model trained on antibodies generalises to nanobodies at all

blocks.html: a part of a chain that folds independently and could, in principle, be cut out and still work. A large protein is a string of domains.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the part of HER2 outside the cell is made of four domains, numbered I to IV.
blocks.context: the unit the competition experiment resolves an epitope down to

blocks.html: how much of a residue is exposed to water, in square ångströms. Computed from a structure, not from sequence.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a residue with near-zero SASA is buried in the core and cannot be part of an interface.
blocks.context: the standard way to turn a structure into a per-residue exposure number

blocks.html: a residue with little or no solvent-accessible surface. It cannot touch another protein, so it can be excluded from interface prediction if a structure is available.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the hydrophobic core of a VHH is buried; the CDR loop tips are not.
blocks.context: the cheapest true-negative filter, available only once a structure exists

blocks.html: a covalent staple between two cysteine residues (C) that pins distant parts of a chain together. Antibody domains have a conserved one; many VHHs have an extra one tying CDR3 down.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: cysteines appear as C in the sequence string and are therefore visible without a structure.
blocks.context: a sequence-visible constraint on CDR3 geometry

blocks.html: one residue replaced by a different one, at one position. The elementary difference between two related sequences.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: position 57 is S in one library member and T in another.
blocks.context: what distinguishes members of a sequence cluster

chapters.title: Antibodies, and why a VHH is the simple case

blocks.html: a protein an immune system makes to recognise one specific target. The classic form is four chains — two heavy, two light — arranged in a Y.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: trastuzumab and pertuzumab, both named in the dataset's column headers, are antibodies.
blocks.context: the class the challenge's binders belong to

blocks.html: the longer of the two chain types in a classic antibody. Two per antibody.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the "H" in VHH refers to the heavy chain.
blocks.context: needed only to explain what a VHH is missing

blocks.html: the shorter chain type in a classic antibody. Two per antibody. A VHH has none — that is the whole point of it.
blocks.context: the half of a normal antibody a VHH does without

blocks.html: the domain at the tip of an antibody arm whose sequence differs from antibody to antibody. It is what does the recognising. Written VH on the heavy chain and VL on the light chain.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a VHH is a variable domain, standing alone.
blocks.context: the only part of an antibody this challenge models

blocks.html: a domain whose sequence is the same across all antibodies of a class. It does the downstream immune signalling and carries no target specificity, so it is absent from this problem entirely.
blocks.context: named so you recognise it as irrelevant here, not because we use it

blocks.html: the beta-sandwich fold every antibody variable domain adopts: two sheets of beta strands face to face, with loops at one end.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a VHH's framework is this fold; its CDR loops are the loops at one end of it.
blocks.context: why framework and loop positions are predictable from sequence alignment alone

blocks.html: an antibody produced as a single, identical molecule rather than as a mixture. Clinical antibody drugs are monoclonals.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the dataset's blocking conditions use three of them — trastuzumab, pertuzumab and a rabbit monoclonal.
blocks.context: what the competition columns pre-block HER2 with

blocks.html: a complete binder that is one variable domain on one chain, about 120 residues. Camelids (llamas, alpacas, camels) make antibodies that have no light chain at all, and the lone heavy-chain variable domain is a VHH. For this challenge it is the best possible case: the entire binder is one string.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the sequence column of AVIDa-hHER2.csv holds one VHH per row; the published ONU1 row starts MAQVQLQESGGGLVQAGGSLRLSCAAS….
blocks.context: the binder half of every record in both tracks

blocks.html: the animal family (llama, alpaca, camel) whose immune systems produce heavy-chain-only antibodies, and therefore VHHs.
blocks.context: where the library's sequences ultimately come from

blocks.html: the conserved scaffold parts of a variable domain, numbered FR1 to FR4. They hold the loops in place and barely vary between library members, which makes them easy to recognise and poor at explaining why one binder works and another does not.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: QVQLQESGGG… is the canonical opening of VHH framework 1, and it is visible at the start of the published ONU1 sequence.
blocks.context: the anchor used to locate the CDR loops inside a raw sequence string

blocks.html: one of the three hypervariable loops of a variable domain: CDR1, CDR2, CDR3. They sit side by side at one end of the fold and form most of the binding surface. "Complementarity-determining" means "the part shaped to fit the target".
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a VHH's layout along its sequence is FR1 · CDR1 · FR2 · CDR2 · FR3 · CDR3 · FR4.
blocks.context: the strongest sequence-only prior available for Track A's binder side

blocks.html: the third and most variable loop, encoded in a way that lets it vary enormously in both length and sequence. In VHHs it is usually the longest loop and often does most of the binding, sometimes reaching into pockets a classic antibody cannot.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: CDR3 length varies between library members while FR1 does not — which is exactly why clusters differ mostly in CDR3.
blocks.context: the loop a competition-stratified analysis should look at first

blocks.html: describing a region whose sequence differs far more between family members than the surrounding regions. Literally: high entropy per column once the sequences are aligned.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: in an aligned set of VHHs, CDR3 columns carry many different letters, FR2 columns carry nearly one.
blocks.context: how CDRs are found computationally when no numbering scheme is applied

blocks.html: the unmutated starting sequence an immune system builds a binder from, before it tunes it. Library members that share a germline look alike in their framework.
blocks.context: one explanation of why cluster structure exists in the dataset

blocks.html: an agreed way of assigning position numbers to antibody residues so that "position 52" means the same structural place in every antibody, regardless of loop length. Three are in common use: Kabat, Chothia and IMGT. They disagree, including about where each CDR starts and ends.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: IMGT inserts gaps so CDR3 always occupies the same numbered window however long it is.
blocks.context: a choice this repository has not yet made; whichever the organisers' templates imply is the one that must be used

blocks.html: the whole collection of distinct binder sequences available in one experiment. Millions of distinct VHHs, most of which bind nothing.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: AVIDa-hHER2.csv is 499 MB — one row per distinct library member.
blocks.context: the population the screen samples from

blocks.html: one distinct sequence in a library, and all the copies of it. Used interchangeably with "library member" in screening papers.
blocks.context: the word a screening paper will use where this dataset says ONU

Left to right is N-terminus to C-terminus, the order the string is written in.

blocks.html: the protein being recognised. In this challenge it is fixed: HER2.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: every record pairs a different VHH with the same antigen.
blocks.context: the target chain of every record

blocks.html: the molecule doing the recognising; here, a VHH. This repository uses binder and target as the two chain names precisely because "antibody/antigen" is one special case of a general two-chain problem.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: SequenceRecord.of({"binder": vhh_seq, "target": her2_seq}).
blocks.context: the chain name in the record type

blocks.html: two or more chains stuck together as one assembly. Track B's output is a predicted complex.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "the HER2–VHH complex" means the two chains positioned correctly relative to each other.
blocks.context: Track B's deliverable

blocks.html: two proteins holding onto each other through many weak contacts at once. No covalent bond is formed; it is reversible, and it is a matter of degree, not a boolean — which is why the dataset has scores rather than flags.
blocks.context: why binary_label is a derived threshold rather than a direct observation

blocks.html: a pair of residues, one from each chain, close enough to be touching. "Close enough" is a convention that has to be stated: a common one is any heavy atom of residue A within about 4.5–5 Å of any heavy atom of residue B. CAPRI's fnat uses a heavy-atom criterion of this kind. The exact cutoff the organisers score with must be read off their README before anything is built on it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 1 Å (ångström) is 0.1 nanometres; a 5 Å cutoff is roughly "two residues' worth of space".
blocks.context: the definition that decides what counts as a positive residue

blocks.html: the set of contacts between two chains in a complex, taken together. The patch where the two proteins meet.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a typical antibody–antigen interface involves on the order of a dozen or two residues per side — a literature regularity, to verify against the structures this challenge is scored on.
blocks.context: the object both tracks are ultimately about

blocks.html: a residue that participates in at least one contact. This is the positive class of Track A: for a given pair of sequences, label every residue 1 if it is an interface residue and 0 otherwise.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: of ~120 VHH residues, only the handful in the CDR loops will be positives — so positives are a small minority.
blocks.context: the prediction target of Track A

blocks.html: the interface residues on the antigen (here, on HER2). The patch of HER2 that is being gripped.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the competition columns distinguish VHHs whose epitope overlaps trastuzumab's site from those whose epitope does not.
blocks.context: what the blocking experiment gives coarse evidence about

blocks.html: the interface residues on the binder (here, on the VHH). The grip itself. Mostly, but not only, inside the CDR loops.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a paratope that lies entirely in CDR3 is common for VHHs — a literature regularity, to verify.
blocks.context: the VHH half of Track A's answer

blocks.html: the interface as a boolean matrix of shape len(binder) × len(target): cell (i, j) is true when residue i of the binder contacts residue j of the antigen. Collapse it along either axis with a logical OR and you get that chain's interface residues.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: for a 120-residue VHH against a 600-residue antigen construct the matrix is 120 × 600 and almost entirely false.
blocks.context: the richest form of a Track A answer; the per-residue vectors are its two marginals

blocks.legendHtml: blue = the full boolean matrix, neutral machinery; green = the two per-residue vectors that are the goal of Track A. The arrows are logical ORs along one axis: the map is the richer object and both vectors are derivable from it, never the other way round.

blocks.html: how tightly a binder holds its target, usually reported as a dissociation constant KD. Smaller is tighter. It is a physical measurement; this dataset does not contain one.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: nanomolar (nM) affinity is strong, micromolar (µM) is weak — three orders of magnitude apart.
blocks.context: named to make clear what the dataset's scores are not

blocks.html: apparent tightness gained by binding at several points at once, rather than by any single grip being stronger. It inflates measured binding in multivalent formats.
blocks.context: a standard confounder in display screens

blocks.html: the degree to which a binder grips its intended target and not other proteins. Measured by comparing binding against the target with binding against something else.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the dataset's Comparator conditions use a non-HER2 protein exactly for this.
blocks.context: what the comparator columns test

blocks.html: the failure mode specificity is tested for: a binder that also grips something it was not meant to.
blocks.context: why a comparator condition exists at all

blocks.html: an epitope made of residues that are consecutive in the sequence.
blocks.context: the easy case, and the rarer one

blocks.html: an epitope made of residues that are far apart in the sequence but brought together by the fold. Most real epitopes are of this kind, which is precisely why a sequence-only model has to learn something about structure to find them.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: residues 20, 95 and 180 of a chain can be neighbours in space and distant in the string.
blocks.context: the core difficulty of sequence-in interface prediction

blocks.html: pre-occupying a known site on the antigen with a known antibody, then asking whether the binder under test can still attach. If it cannot, its epitope overlaps the blocker's site.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the Her2_Trastuzumab_* conditions are HER2 pre-blocked with trastuzumab.
blocks.context: the experiment that turns a sequence-level screen into coarse region-level epitope evidence

blocks.html: a group of binders that compete with each other, and therefore probably share a region of the antigen. A coarse, experimentally derived partition of the antigen surface.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "blocked by trastuzumab" and "blocked by pertuzumab" are two bins the dataset's columns can define.
blocks.context: the stratification variable this challenge's competition columns make available

chapters.title: HER2 — the antigen in this challenge

blocks.html: Everything in this chapter about where an antibody binds is a literature claim: it comes from published structures, not from anything measured in this repository. It is flagged as such on every entry and must be checked against the published complexes before any pipeline depends on it.

a statement taken from published work rather than from a run in this repository. House rule: it is written as a claim, named as such, and carries what would have to be read to confirm it. It is never promoted to a repo fact by repetition.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "trastuzumab binds HER2 domain IV" is a literature claim until checked against the deposited structure.
blocks.context: the discipline the challenge page applies to every biology prior it uses

blocks.html: a protein that sits in a cell's outer membrane, with one part outside the cell and one part inside, and passes a signal across when something attaches outside.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: HER2 is one.
blocks.context: what kind of protein the antigen is

blocks.html: the part of a receptor that is outside the cell. It is the only part an antibody in the bloodstream can reach, and therefore the only part this challenge cares about.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: HER2's ectodomain is the four-domain region antibodies bind.
blocks.context: the antigen construct a screen actually uses

blocks.html: a receptor whose inside-the-cell part is an enzyme that switches on growth signalling when the outside part is engaged. The family HER2 belongs to.
blocks.context: why HER2 is a cancer drug target

blocks.term: HER2 (ERBB2, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2)
aliases: ERBB2, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2
blocks.html: the antigen for this whole challenge. A receptor tyrosine kinase, over-produced in a subset of breast and gastric cancers, and the target of several approved antibody drugs. Fixed across every record: the challenge varies the binder, not the target.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: every condition column prefixed Her2_ is a selection round against this protein.
blocks.context: the target chain of every record in both tracks

blocks.html: the four domains of the HER2 ectodomain, numbered I to IV from the end furthest from the membrane to the end nearest it. Different antibodies bind different subdomains, which is what makes competition informative.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: domain IV is the membrane-proximal one; domain II carries the dimerisation arm.
blocks.context: the resolution at which a competition experiment can place an epitope

blocks.html: a protruding loop on HER2 domain II through which HER2 pairs up with another receptor. Blocking it blocks the pairing.
blocks.context: the site pertuzumab is reported to occupy

blocks.html: a clinical anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody. Literature claim: it binds the membrane-proximal subdomain IV. Appears in the dataset as six blocking conditions.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Marin-Her2_Trastuzumab_C1_37C-1st-B is one of them.
blocks.context: one of the three blockers whose competition columns can bin an epitope

blocks.html: a second clinical anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody. Literature claim: it binds the dimerisation arm on subdomain II — a different, non-overlapping site from trastuzumab's. Appears in the dataset as two blocking conditions.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Marin-Her2_Pertuzumab_C3_37C-1st-B and Marin-Her2_Pertuzumab_C3_4C-1st-B.
blocks.context: the second blocker; the non-overlap with trastuzumab is what makes two bins rather than one

blocks.html: a third blocking antibody in the dataset, raised in rabbit. Its epitope is not stated in anything we have, so it defines a third bin whose location is unknown.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Marin-Her2_RabMAb_C3_37C-1st-B.
blocks.context: a third blocking site, useful as a partition even while unlocated

blocks.html: a non-HER2 protein included in the screen so that binding to HER2 can be distinguished from binding to anything protein-shaped. Its identity is not stated in anything we have.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the four Marin-Comparator_* columns.
blocks.context: the specificity control of the screen

chapters.title: How the data was made — selection screens

blocks.html: The dataset is not a list of measured affinities. It is a record of who survived a selection, counted by sequencing. Understanding that shape is what tells you which columns can be trusted and for what.

the laboratory technique that physically links a protein to the DNA that encodes it, so that selecting the protein also selects its sequence. Phage display, yeast display and ribosome display are the common variants. Which one produced this dataset is not stated in anything we have — to confirm from the organisers' README.
blocks.context: the mechanism that makes a sequencing read count a binding signal

blocks.html: one cycle of the screen: expose the whole library to the immobilised antigen, wash away what does not stick, keep what does, amplify it, repeat.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the dataset's condition names carry 1st and 2nd, which read as first and second round.
blocks.context: what a "round" in a column name refers to

blocks.html: one iteration of panning. Later rounds are more enriched for real binders and less diverse; early rounds are noisier but broader.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Marin-Her2_C1_37C-2nd-B is a second-round condition.
blocks.context: one axis of the condition-column grammar

blocks.html: the increase in a sequence's share of the library from one round to the next. A binder's share rises; a non-binder's falls. This is the actual signal in the data.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a sequence going from 1 read in 10 million to 10,000 reads in 10 million is enriched.
blocks.context: what every score column in the dataset is derived from

blocks.html: a number summarising enrichment for one sequence under one condition, usually on a log scale and usually normalised against a reference condition. The dataset's IE columns are of this kind.
blocks.context: the derived quantity the dataset's labels are built from

blocks.html: a condition run with no antigen present, so that whatever enriches anyway is enriching for a reason that has nothing to do with the target: sticking to plastic, growing faster, surviving the wash.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the seven Marin-NC* columns.
blocks.context: the baseline every target score has to be read against

blocks.html: the same condition run more than once, so that the difference between runs estimates the noise. The trailing B and C in the dataset's condition names read as replicate labels.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Marin-Her2_C1_37C-2nd-B and Marin-Her2_C1_37C-2nd-C differ only in that letter.
blocks.context: the only handle on measurement noise the dataset offers

blocks.html: one combination of antigen, blocker, temperature, round and replicate: one column of the dataset's score block. 26 of them.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the name grammar reads as Marin-<condition>[_C<n>]_<temp>-<round>-<rep>.
blocks.context: the columns a feature-engineering pass has to interpret before it can use them

blocks.html: the C1 / C2 / C3 index in the condition names. Whether it denotes a campaign, a chamber or a clone is not stated in anything we have — to confirm.
blocks.context: an unresolved axis of the column grammar; it matters because it decides what may be averaged together

blocks.html: a screen run against antigen that has been pre-blocked, so that only binders with a non-overlapping epitope can enrich. Comparing the blocked and unblocked conditions for the same sequence is the epitope signal.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the ratio Her2_Trastuzumab_* / Her2_* is, if the column names mean what they appear to mean, a coarse epitope label computable from the table alone.
blocks.context: the one structural signal recoverable without any external data; stated as a hypothesis, not a measured result

blocks.html: reading millions of DNA fragments in parallel. The readout of the whole screen: after selection, sequence everything and count.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: NGS_read_count_table.csv, 126 MB.
blocks.context: how the surviving library becomes a table

blocks.html: one sequence fragment the sequencer reported. The raw unit of NGS output.
blocks.context: the unit summed into every count in the dataset

blocks.html: how many reads matched a given sequence in a given condition. The raw observation behind every derived score; a count, so it is noisy in a way proportional to its size and zero is not the same as "absent".
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the published ONU1 row carries total = 23,939 reads across the experiment.
blocks.context: the quantity the IE scores are computed from

blocks.html: how many reads a condition produced in total. Two conditions with different depths are not directly comparable until counts are normalised into shares.
blocks.context: the normalisation that has to happen before any two columns are compared

blocks.html: a systematic difference between runs that has nothing to do with biology: different depth, different day, different operator. It will be confounded with anything that varies along the same axis.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the 37C / 4C and B / C axes in the column names are where to look for one.
blocks.context: the first thing a profiling pass should test for, once the data is downloaded

blocks.html: a label that is correct about something adjacent to what you want to predict. The dataset's labels say that a VHH binds HER2; the task asks where. That gap is the central difficulty of this challenge and must be named in the report, not papered over.
blocks.context: the exact relationship between this dataset and this task

blocks.legendHtml: purple = the raw input library; yellow = the selection step, the decision the experiment makes; green = sequences that survive it; blue = the counting and scoring machinery that produces the published columns; red on the left = sequences lost in the wash, red on the right = the gap: the pipeline ends at a sequence-level score and the task needs a residue-level answer. Nothing in the chain carries residue information, which is why weak supervision or transfer from structural data is unavoidable.

blocks.html: Everything in this chapter is read off the published schema quoted in challenge.md. The files are not downloaded and nothing here has been measured. Items marked to confirm are unresolved against the organisers' own README.

the challenge dataset: a 499 MB table of VHH sequences screened against HER2, plus a 126 MB NGS count table, three prediction templates and a README. Renamed by the organisers from ONU_table_mod_IE_score_arranged_with_cluster_all.csv.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the file set is AVIDa-hHER2.csv (499 MB), NGS_read_count_table.csv (126 MB), prediction_template_ONU11.csv, prediction_template_ONU13.csv, prediction_template_ONU23.csv, README.md (17.3 kB), an empty LICENSE and .gitattributes.
blocks.context: the only dataset in this challenge

blocks.html: the organisers' identifier for one distinct sequence in the library. What the abbreviation expands to is not stated in anything we have — to confirm from the organisers' README. Functionally it is the primary key.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ONU1, ONU11, ONU13, ONU23.
blocks.context: the row key of the main table and the name of each prediction template

blocks.html: the #ONU ID column: the row key of AVIDa-hHER2.csv. Note the leading #, which many CSV readers will treat as a comment character unless told not to.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ONU1.
blocks.context: the join key between the main table, the count table and the templates

blocks.html: the total read count for one sequence across the whole experiment.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the published ONU1 row has total = 23,939.
blocks.context: the obvious confidence weight — a score derived from few reads is a noisy score

blocks.html: the column holding the VHH amino-acid string.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the published ONU1 value begins MAQVQLQESGGGLVQAGGSLRLSCAASGGTVSTFDMGWFRQAPGKEREFVSRISWDHGTTRYADSVKGRFTISRDDAKNTVYLQLNSLKAEDTAV.
blocks.context: the model input for the binder half of every record

blocks.html: the dataset's enrichment statistic, carried in two columns. What IE abbreviates is not stated in anything we have — to confirm from the organisers' README. It reads as an enrichment index; it is not an affinity.
blocks.context: the derived quantity the labels are built from

blocks.html: the background_IE_score column: enrichment against the background and control conditions. High here means "enriches for reasons unrelated to HER2".
blocks.context: the denominator any honest target signal has to beat

blocks.html: the target_IE_score column: enrichment against the HER2 conditions.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the published ONU1 row carries the sentinel -500 here.
blocks.context: the primary binding signal in the table

blocks.html: a string class label. noise is one observed value; the full set of values is not stated in anything we have — to confirm.
blocks.context: a categorical annotation whose vocabulary must be read before it is used

blocks.html: the binary_label column: the binder / non-binder target, as a float. How it is derived from the IE scores is not stated in anything we have — to confirm. It is null in the published example row, so nullability is real and must be handled.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: null in the published ONU1 row.
blocks.context: the sequence-level supervision signal; weak with respect to the residue-level task

blocks.html: the Cluster column: a sequence-family assignment grouping near-identical library members together. Also present as a numeric #Cluster.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Cluster1.
blocks.context: the grouping key every train/test split must respect

blocks.html: the Cluster_size column: how many library members are in that cluster. Large clusters are the leakage hazard.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the published example cluster has Cluster_size = 5,378.
blocks.context: the number that makes a random row split obviously wrong

blocks.html: a reserved number standing in for "no value", inside a column typed as a number. This dataset uses -500. Treating it as a real score would wreck every downstream statistic silently — an explicit missing-data policy is required before any modelling.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: -500 appears in the published ONU1 row in several condition columns and in target_IE_score.
blocks.context: the single highest-risk data-quality item in the dataset

blocks.html: one of the 26 float columns prefixed Marin-, each holding a score for one sequence under one experimental condition, grouped as negative control, comparator, plain HER2, and HER2 pre-blocked with RabMAb, pertuzumab or trastuzumab.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Marin-Her2_Trastuzumab_C2_4C-1st-B.
blocks.context: the raw per-condition evidence behind the two IE scores, and the source of the competition signal

blocks.html: the submission file the organisers supply, one per evaluation target, which defines the output contract. What one row of it represents is not stated in anything we have — to confirm; it defines the deliverable.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: three of them — prediction_template_ONU11.csv, prediction_template_ONU13.csv (8.76 kB each) and prediction_template_ONU23.csv (8.85 kB).
blocks.context: the shape of what is actually scored

blocks.html: one of the three VHHs predictions are requested for: ONU11, ONU13, ONU23. The 499 MB table is derivation material; these three are the thing being scored.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: three templates of about 8.8 kB each, which is on the order of a few hundred rows.
blocks.context: the reason internal validation must be far broader than the official metric — three targets is a tiny test set

blocks.html: NGS_read_count_table.csv, 126 MB: the per-run counts. What it holds that the main table does not is an open question — presumably the raw counts behind the IE scores.
blocks.context: the lower-level view, useful for recomputing a score rather than trusting one

blocks.html: an input number a model is allowed to look at. Turning a sequence into features is most of the engineering.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "is this residue hydrophobic", "is this position inside CDR3", "what did a language model embed this position as".
blocks.context: the interface between the biology and the model

blocks.html: the answer a prediction is scored against. For Track A it is the true interface residues of the three evaluation targets; the dataset's own columns are not ground truth for that.
blocks.context: what the challenge grades against, as distinct from what the dataset supervises on

blocks.html: fitting a model on examples where the answer is known, so it can answer on examples where it is not.
blocks.context: the default framing; weakened here because the known answers are at the wrong granularity

blocks.html: the examples the model is allowed to fit on.
blocks.context: one of three disjoint partitions

blocks.html: examples held back from fitting, used to choose between models and settings. Looking at it too often turns it into a training set by proxy.
blocks.context: where model selection happens

blocks.html: examples touched once, at the end, to estimate real performance. Here the official one is three VHHs, which is far too small to distinguish close models — so an internal test set has to carry the real weight.
blocks.context: the official three targets, plus whatever internal held-out set we construct

blocks.html: performing on data the model has not seen. The only thing that counts.
blocks.context: the property every split decision is protecting

blocks.html: learning the training examples rather than the pattern. Visible as good training scores and poor held-out scores.
blocks.context: the ordinary failure; leakage is the sneaky one, because it hides overfitting

blocks.html: information from the test set reaching the model during training, so the reported score measures memory instead of prediction. It does not announce itself: the scores simply look good.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: putting two near-identical sequences from the same cluster on opposite sides of a split.
blocks.context: the single easiest way to get a confidently wrong answer in this challenge

blocks.html: the percentage of positions at which two aligned sequences carry the same residue. The standard measure of "how related are these two".
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: two VHHs differing only in three CDR3 positions are well above 90 % identical.
blocks.context: the quantity a clustering threshold is set on

blocks.html: grouping sequences so that everything within a group is above a chosen identity threshold. The usual tools are CD-HIT and MMseqs2. This dataset ships its own clustering in the Cluster column, so the grouping does not have to be recomputed — but the threshold the organisers used is not stated anywhere we have, and it governs how strong the leakage protection is.
blocks.context: how the grouping key for a safe split is produced

blocks.html: assigning rows to train and test independently at random. Wrong here. With clusters in the thousands, near-identical sequences land on both sides and the reported score measures recall of the training set.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: one published cluster has 5,378 members — a random split puts most of them in training and some in test.
blocks.context: the baseline mistake this challenge punishes

blocks.html: assigning whole clusters, never rows, to train, validation and test. Every member of a cluster goes to the same side. This is the correct split for this dataset and is non-negotiable.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: GroupKFold with Cluster as the group, rather than KFold over rows.
blocks.context: the standing rule for every experiment on this dataset

blocks.html: one class being far rarer than the other. Here the positive class — interface residues — is a small minority of all residues, which breaks accuracy as a metric and flatters ROC AUC.
blocks.context: the reason the challenge scores Track A with PR AUC

blocks.html: the fraction of examples that are positive. It is also the PR AUC a random model achieves, which makes it the only honest floor to compare against.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: arithmetic, not a measurement — if 12 of 120 residues are interface, the base rate is 0.10, so a PR AUC of 0.10 is worth nothing and 0.35 is worth something.
blocks.context: the number every reported PR AUC must be quoted beside

blocks.html: telling the loss function to care more about the rare class, so the model does not minimise error by predicting "negative" everywhere.
blocks.context: the standard first response to imbalance

blocks.html: whether a predicted probability means what it says: of the residues scored 0.7, about 70 % should be interface. A model can rank well and be badly calibrated.
blocks.context: required if per-residue probabilities are submitted rather than a binary map

blocks.html: training on labels that are cheap, plentiful and only indirectly related to the target, instead of scarce exact ones. The frame this entire challenge sits in: millions of sequence-level binding labels, zero residue-level ones.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: deriving a coarse epitope bin from the competition columns and training on that, rather than on true contacts.
blocks.context: the central methodological choice of Track A

blocks.html: reusing what a model learned on one problem for a different one. Here: learn from the large public set of solved protein complexes, apply to these three.
blocks.context: the alternative, or complement, to weak supervision

blocks.html: the first, large, self-supervised stage of training, on data with no task labels at all. For proteins: predict masked residues across hundreds of millions of sequences.
blocks.context: where a protein language model's knowledge comes from

blocks.html: continuing to train a pre-trained model on the specific task, usually with far less data.
blocks.context: the step that would consume this dataset's weak labels

blocks.html: using a pre-trained model on a task it was never trained for, with no fitting at all. Cheap, honest, and the right first baseline.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: reading contact-like signal straight out of a language model without fitting anything on AVIDa-hHER2.
blocks.context: the baseline a trained model has to beat to justify itself

blocks.html: a transformer trained on raw protein sequences, which ends up encoding structural and functional properties it was never shown. The ESM family is the best-known example. It turns a sequence into a vector per residue.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a lane with input_class = "sequence" in this repository's roster is a model of this kind.
blocks.context: the likely backbone of a sequence-only Track A model

blocks.html: the vector a model produces for one residue (or one whole sequence), carrying what the model knows about it. The usual bridge between a pre-trained model and a small task-specific head.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: one vector per residue, concatenated with hand-made features before a classifier.
blocks.context: the feature representation a per-residue classifier would consume

blocks.html: the matrix of how much each position of a transformer's input attended to each other position. Literature claim, to verify: some attention heads in protein language models correlate with residue contacts, making them a zero-shot contact signal.
blocks.context: a cheap candidate source of contact structure; must be validated before being believed

blocks.html: many related sequences stacked so that equivalent positions line up in columns. Gaps are inserted to make lengths match.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: aligning the members of one Cluster reveals which columns vary and which do not.
blocks.context: the classical input to co-evolution analysis, and still an input to several structure predictors

blocks.html: the observation that positions in contact tend to mutate together across evolution, because a change in one must be compensated by a change in the other. Reading contacts out of an alignment this way is the idea modern structure prediction grew out of.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: columns i and j of an MSA whose letters covary are candidate contacts.
blocks.context: why an MSA carries structural information at all

blocks.html: the simplest method you compare everything against. A result without one is not a result.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "predict every CDR residue as interface and nothing else" is the obvious baseline for Track A's binder side.
blocks.context: required beside every reported metric in this repository

blocks.html: a setting chosen rather than fitted: learning rate, threshold, number of layers. Chosen on validation data, never on test data.
blocks.context: what the validation set exists for

blocks.html: repeating train/validate over several different partitions and averaging, to get a less luck-dependent estimate. Here it must be grouped by cluster, like every other split.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 5-fold GroupKFold with Cluster as the group.
blocks.context: the internal evaluation protocol, given a three-target official test set

blocks.html: keeping the proportions of a variable the same across splits, or analysing each of its levels separately. Here the natural variable is the epitope bin.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: reporting Track A metrics per epitope bin rather than pooled.
blocks.context: how the competition signal is used for evaluation rather than for training

blocks.html: running a trained model to get predictions. Distinct from training; in this repository every model is used at inference only, never trained.
blocks.context: all the zoo does

blocks.html: combining several models' predictions. Usually beats any single member, and gives a cheap disagreement signal.
blocks.context: the natural use of a zoo of independent lanes

chapters.title: Metrics — how a per-residue prediction is scored

blocks.html: the 2 × 2 table of predicted class against true class: true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives. Every metric below is a ratio out of this table.
blocks.context: the common ancestor of precision, recall and the rest

blocks.html: predicted interface, and really interface.
blocks.context: the numerator of both precision and recall

blocks.html: predicted interface, actually not. Under heavy imbalance these are abundant and they are what destroys precision.
blocks.context: the dominant error type in an imbalanced problem

blocks.html: a real interface residue the model missed.
blocks.context: the error recall counts

blocks.html: the cutoff that turns a probability into a decision. Every point on a precision–recall curve is one threshold.
blocks.context: the free parameter PR AUC integrates away

blocks.html: of the residues the model called interface, what fraction really are: TP / (TP + FP). "When it speaks, is it right?"
blocks.context: one axis of the Track A metric

blocks.html: of the residues that really are interface, what fraction the model found: TP / (TP + FN). "Does it find everything?"
blocks.context: the other axis of the Track A metric

blocks.html: of the residues that are not interface, what fraction the model correctly left alone. Also called specificity — a different sense of the word from binding specificity in chapter 3, and a frequent source of confusion.
blocks.context: named to disambiguate it from the binding sense of specificity

blocks.html: the harmonic mean of precision and recall, at one chosen threshold. A single number, but it hides the threshold choice.
blocks.context: a reasonable secondary report; never a substitute for the curve

blocks.html: precision plotted against recall as the threshold sweeps from strict to permissive. It shows the whole trade-off instead of one point on it.
blocks.context: the curve the Track A metric integrates

blocks.term: PR AUC (area under the precision–recall curve)
blocks.html: the Track A primary metric. One number summarising the whole precision–recall curve; also reported as average precision. Its floor is not 0.5 — it is the positive rate, so it must always be quoted next to that rate.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: arithmetic, not a measurement — at a 10 % positive rate, a random model scores about 0.10, so "PR AUC 0.30" means three times random, not "30 % right".
blocks.context: the number Track A is ranked on

blocks.html: true positive rate against false positive rate as the threshold sweeps. Its false positive rate is divided by the large number of true negatives, which is exactly why it is insensitive to imbalance.
blocks.context: the metric this challenge deliberately does not use

blocks.html: area under the ROC curve. Floor 0.5, ceiling 1.0. Misleading under heavy imbalance: a model that is wrong about almost every positive can still score 0.9, because the abundant true negatives dominate the denominator.
blocks.context: why PR AUC was chosen instead

blocks.legendHtml: purple = the raw per-residue examples; yellow = the metric choice, the decision this diagram is about; red = the misleading route, where the abundant true negatives swamp the denominator and flatter a useless model; green = the metric this challenge actually scores Track A with. TPR is the true positive rate (recall) and FPR the false positive rate.

blocks.html: a single correlation-like score between prediction and truth, between -1 and +1, that uses all four cells of the confusion matrix and stays meaningful under imbalance.
blocks.context: the best single-number secondary metric to report beside PR AUC

blocks.html: of the k residues the model is most confident about, what fraction are really interface. Matches how a predicted epitope is actually used: you follow up a short list, not a probability field.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: with k set to the known interface size, this is the natural "did it find the patch" score.
blocks.context: a practically meaningful companion metric to PR AUC

blocks.html: scoring each residue of each chain as its own example. Track A's shape.
blocks.context: the granularity Track A is scored at

blocks.html: scoring each predicted complex as one example, with a structural quality measure. Track B's shape.
blocks.context: the granularity Track B is scored at

blocks.html: compute the metric separately per target, then average the results. Every target counts equally, however many residues it has.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: with three evaluation targets, a macro average is the mean of three PR AUCs.
blocks.context: the right default when targets differ in length and in interface size

blocks.html: pool every residue from every target into one set and compute the metric once. A long target then dominates.
blocks.context: stated so the choice between the two is made deliberately and reported

blocks.html: the organisers' ranking of submissions. With three evaluation targets, a gap of one or two residues is noise, so a leaderboard position is weak evidence about a method.
blocks.context: why internal validation must be broader than the official metric

blocks.html: the public archive of experimentally determined protein structures, including thousands of antibody–antigen complexes. The source of real interface labels, and therefore the transfer-learning well everything draws from.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a deposited HER2–trastuzumab complex is what the chapter-4 literature claims would be checked against.
blocks.context: where structural ground truth comes from, since this dataset carries none

blocks.html: one deposited structure, named by a four-character identifier. It contains coordinates, chain identifiers and the experiment's metadata.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: identifiers look like 1N8Z — four characters, letters and digits.
blocks.context: the unit a structural training set is assembled from

blocks.html: the two text formats a structure is distributed in. The legacy PDB format is column-positional and capped in size; mmCIF is the modern replacement — a bundle of named tables in one text file, a loop_ header listing column names followed by whitespace-separated data rows. In software terms, mmCIF is a CSV whose delimiter is \s+ and whose header rows are named.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this repository has a tokeniser for it in src/sepiq/viz/mmcif_tokens.py, which handles bare values, quoted values and multi-line ; text fields.
blocks.context: the format any predicted structure will be written in and any reference structure read from
blocks.source: the mmCIF specification, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: one row of a structure file: which atom, in which residue, of which chain, at which x/y/z coordinate.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the mmCIF table _atom_site holds these, one row per atom.
blocks.context: the elementary content of a structure file
blocks.source: the mmCIF specification, no repo owner yet

blocks.html: any atom except hydrogen. Most structure files omit hydrogens entirely, so contact definitions are stated over heavy atoms.
blocks.context: the atom set a contact cutoff is measured over

blocks.html: the one backbone atom present in every residue, often used as that residue's single representative position. Coarse but convenient.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a "CA-only RMSD" compares one point per residue instead of all atoms.
blocks.context: the usual simplification when a per-residue distance is needed

blocks.html: the letter naming one chain inside a structure file. Which letter is the binder and which the antigen is a per-file convention and a classic source of silently swapped inputs.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this repository avoids the problem by naming chains binder and target rather than positionally.
blocks.context: why the record type uses named chains

blocks.html: the residue numbers the depositor chose, which need not start at 1, need not be contiguous, and need not match the sequence index. Mapping between author numbering and sequence position is a required, error-prone step.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a structure may number its first modelled residue 23 because residues 1–22 were not resolved.
blocks.context: the join every structure-derived label has to survive

blocks.html: rotating and translating one structure onto another so the compared parts overlap as well as possible. Every structural comparison starts with a choice of what to superpose on, and that choice is what distinguishes the metrics below.
blocks.context: the step before any RMSD is computed

blocks.html: after superposition, the square root of the mean squared distance between corresponding atoms. In ångströms; lower is better; 0 is identical.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: it is a plain L2 distance averaged over atom pairs, nothing more exotic than that.
blocks.context: the base measure all three CAPRI distances specialise

blocks.html: superpose on the antigen, then measure how far the binder is from where it should be. Answers "is the binder in the right place on the target".
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a large L-RMSD with a small internal error means the binder is correctly folded and docked to the wrong patch.
blocks.context: one of the three CAPRI measures DockQ combines

blocks.html: the same idea restricted to interface residues and backbone atoms only. Answers "is the contact patch itself geometrically right", ignoring everything away from it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "bb" is backbone; "i" is interface.
blocks.context: one of the three CAPRI measures DockQ combines

blocks.html: of the contacts in the true structure, the fraction the prediction reproduces. Between 0 and 1; a set-overlap measure, not a distance.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: it is recall computed over contact pairs rather than residues.
blocks.context: the contact-level member of the CAPRI trio, and the one that connects Track B back to Track A

blocks.html: a single score from 0 to 1 combining fnat, L-RMSD and i-RMSD into one number. The headline Track B metric.
blocks.context: what Track B is ranked on

blocks.html: the long-running community experiment in predicting protein complexes. Its assessment conventions are what Track B borrows.
blocks.context: where the Track B metric vocabulary comes from

blocks.html: the discrete verdict a prediction is placed in: incorrect, acceptable,
blocks.exampleHtml: medium or high. Literature claim, to verify against the organisers' scorer: the published DockQ bands are incorrect below 0.23, acceptable from 0.23, medium from 0.49 and high from 0.80.
blocks.context: how a continuous DockQ is reported as a verdict; the thresholds must be confirmed before being quoted as ours

blocks.html: predicting how two known structures fit together. Distinct from folding, which predicts one structure from one sequence. Both tracks here start from sequence, so a full stack has to fold then dock, or do both at once.
blocks.context: the second half of a Track B pipeline

blocks.html: one candidate arrangement of the two chains. A docking run produces many; choosing between them is a separate problem from generating them.
blocks.context: what a scoring function ranks

blocks.html: the model that ranks poses. Generating a near-correct pose and failing to rank it first is a common and separately diagnosable failure.
blocks.context: the half of docking that the competition columns could supply an independent check on

blocks.html: an externally supplied constraint that poses must satisfy, used to cut the search space. The competition columns can supply one: reject poses that put the binder in the wrong HER2 subdomain.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: "the epitope must lie in domain II" for a pertuzumab-blocked binder — conditional on the literature claim about pertuzumab's site holding.
blocks.context: the practical use of the competition signal in Track B

blocks.html: predicting a chain's tertiary structure from its sequence alone. AlphaFold-class and Boltz-class models do this, some of them for complexes directly. No model has been chosen for this challenge: the roster in this repository is deliberately empty.
blocks.context: the first stage of any structure-routed approach; the choice is still open

blocks.html: a structure predictor's own per-residue confidence, 0–100, higher meaning more certain. Low pLDDT regions are often genuinely flexible loops rather than prediction failures — which, for a CDR3, is information rather than noise.
blocks.context: a per-residue confidence signal usable as a feature even when the structure is not trusted

blocks.html: a predictor's confidence in the relative position of two parts of a structure. Low PAE between two chains is the usual proxy for "this complex is probably real".
blocks.context: the standard filter on a predicted complex

blocks.html: a predictor's single-number confidence in an interface it predicted. Commonly used to rank candidate complexes.
blocks.context: a ranking signal for Track B poses

blocks.html: a protein's structure when alone (apo) versus when bound to a partner (holo). They differ, sometimes at exactly the residues that matter, which is why predicting each chain alone and then docking rigidly can fail even when both folds are correct.
blocks.context: the standing caveat on any fold-then-dock pipeline

blocks.html: The vocabulary below is this repository's own, and every term matches the code named in its source line. The research domain changed; this layer did not, because it was written to be case-agnostic.

this repository's registry and runner for frozen third-party models, used as interchangeable lanes. Nothing here is trained: one record shape goes in, one score row comes out, and which model produced it is a registry entry rather than a branch in the code.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the package is src/sepiq/zoo/.
blocks.context: the component that will run whatever interface and structure predictors this challenge ends up using

blocks.html: one model, wired in. A new lane is a new adapter module plus a new roster entry, never an edit to a shared file.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the roster is keyed by a short lane key, as in [models.example].
blocks.context: the unit of extension in the zoo

blocks.html: the protocol a lane implements, so a caller never branches on which model it is talking to. It declares name, version, tier and catalogue_adjacent, and offers coverage(), score() for local tiers and submit() for remote ones.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: class Adapter(Protocol) in src/sepiq/zoo/types.py.
blocks.context: the seam between the workflow and any model

blocks.html: where a lane's numbers come from, as a number: 1 = a lookup in a precomputed table, 2 = a local CPU process, 3 = a remote GPU. Tier decides cost, latency and whether the call is synchronous.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Tier = Literal[1, 2, 3].
blocks.context: the cost class of every lane

blocks.html: what a lane reads, declared in its roster entry: sequence (a single chain), pair (two chains whose relationship is the question) or structure (a lane that emits or consumes coordinates). A record set is matched against it, so a lane is never handed input it cannot read.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: INPUT_CLASSES = ("sequence", "pair", "structure").
blocks.context: the declaration that maps this challenge's two tracks onto lanes — Track A is pair, Track B is structure

blocks.html: the unit of work: one item_id, a set of named chains, and open meta. A lane reads only the keys it declares, so adding a field never breaks a lane that does not use it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: SequenceRecord.of({"binder": vhh, "target": her2}, onu="ONU11").
blocks.context: what one row of the dataset becomes before any model sees it

blocks.html: the named sequence strings inside a record: binder and target. Named rather than positional on purpose — an interface model that silently swapped its two inputs would still run and would still produce numbers.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: class Chains(TypedDict, total=False): binder: str; target: str.
blocks.context: the two halves of every record in this challenge

blocks.html: the stable content key of a record: 16 hex characters of SHA-256 over its chain contents in a fixed order. Content-addressed on purpose — two runs that build the same record agree on its id without coordinating, a cached score is a hit for the next run, and a changed input is a different id rather than a silent overwrite.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: item_id("binder=MAQVQ…", "target=…") → 16 hex characters.
blocks.context: the cache key and the only identifier that crosses to a remote lane

blocks.html: one model's verdict on one record: the single summary score, plus aux for anything vector-valued, plus the digest, venue, licence and run_id that make the row auditable.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a Track A lane puts its per-residue probability vector or contact map in aux and a summary number in score.
blocks.context: the one output shape every lane produces

blocks.html: the free-form dictionary on a score row holding everything that is not one number: per-residue probabilities, a contact map, a confidence.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this is where a Track A submission's actual content lives.
blocks.context: where the interesting half of an interface prediction ends up

blocks.html: the hash of the weights or table a lane actually read, recorded on every score row. It is what makes a cached row trustworthy: a lane whose weights changed produces a different digest, so a stale score is visible rather than silently reused.
blocks.context: the integrity check on every cached result

blocks.html: where a score was computed, recorded on the row: laptop, or modal:<gpu>.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: venue = "laptop" is the default on ScoreRow.
blocks.context: part of the reproducibility record of every number

blocks.html: how much of a record set one model can score, reported by class. A lane that scores 40 % of the records is not broken; it is a lane with a stated domain. Coverage is reported next to every result rather than hidden behind a filter.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Coverage(model=…, scored=…, total=…, by_class=…) with a fraction property.
blocks.context: the honesty requirement on every lane's output

The concrete table of lanes against input classes cannot be drawn yet, because no model has been chosen and the roster is empty.

blocks.html: the README of one model: its name, the exact version scored against, where its numbers come from, what its licence allows, and how much of our data it can speak about. A card is a declaration; the adapter it names is what acts.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the roster's fields are name, version, tier, input_class, source, adapter, licence, non_commercial, catalogue_adjacent, scope, enabled, pmid.
blocks.context: what has to be filled in, from the model's own README and licence file, before a lane may be enabled

blocks.html: the shared model table, models.toml, plus one optional fragment per lane in models.d/<key>.toml. A fragment adds a model or overrides fields of one already there, so two people adding two lanes never edit one file; two fragments claiming one key is an error. The roster is currently empty on purpose: no model has been chosen for this challenge, and a card is a claim about a published artefact that must be checked before it is written.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: models.toml contains one disabled template block named Template lane — not a real model.
blocks.context: the current state of model selection — nothing chosen, deliberately

blocks.html: a flag on a model card marking a model trained on the same public structures or complexes the evaluation is drawn from. Such a lane is not excluded, but its agreement with the answer is reported separately, because it may be recall rather than prediction.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a structure predictor trained on PDB complexes, evaluated against a PDB complex, is catalogue-adjacent.
blocks.context: the distinction between a model that knew the answer and a model that worked it out — central to this challenge, since antibody–antigen complexes are well represented in public structure databases

blocks.html: a card field recording that a model's terms forbid commercial use. It changes what may ship, so it is declared rather than discovered.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the registry also generates a licence manifest across every enabled lane.
blocks.context: the licence check that happens before a lane is enabled

blocks.html: a card's rollout bucket: mvp, opt-a or opt-b. mvp is the set of lanes that must work; the others are optional widenings.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: SCOPES = ("mvp", "opt-a", "opt-b").
blocks.context: how lane work is prioritised

blocks.html: the serverless compute platform this repository uses for tier-3 work: run a container on a GPU, pay per second, no cluster to keep alive.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: one app per lane, named sepiq-zoo-<key>.
blocks.context: the venue for every GPU lane

blocks.html: a tier-3 lane: the laptop submits a batch of items, a GPU container scores them, and the reply comes back with the scores, the weights digest the container measured and the GPU seconds it spent. Each lane gets its own app so deploying one never replaces another, and modal app stop can end one lane alone.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: every lane app exposes one class Scorer with one method score_batch.
blocks.context: how a model too large for the laptop gets run

blocks.html: the deliberately minimal contract between the laptop and a GPU container: one call carries a batch of items, each item a content-addressed id plus its named chains. Nothing else crosses the wire — no labels, no grouping keys, nothing the container has no use for.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Item and Reply TypedDicts in src/sepiq/zoo/modal_contract.py.
blocks.context: the data-minimisation rule for remote compute

blocks.html: the per-lane persistent disk a GPU lane keeps its model weights on, so a cold start does not re-download gigabytes. One per lane, named sepiq-zoo-{key}-weights, and listed in the deletion checklist.
blocks.context: the only state a GPU lane keeps between calls

blocks.html: the append-only JSONL file under build/modal/ with one line per remote call, priced from the platform's published per-second GPU rate. It lets a run quote its own cost without trusting a dashboard; the platform's billing report is the reconciliation, and a run quotes both.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: build/modal/ledger.jsonl, one line per call, never edited.
blocks.context: the cost audit trail for every GPU lane

blocks.html: the check asked before every wave of remote calls: would this wave, padded by an overhead factor, push the lane past its share or the step past the cap? A lane that would overrun stops and says so rather than running out of money halfway.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: BudgetExceededError, raised by Ledger.guard.
blocks.context: the stop condition on remote spend

blocks.html: the one reply shape every API route in this repository returns: {data, cached_at, source}. source is not a static description — it is appended with the concrete upstreams and cache key that produced this reply, so a number on a page can be traced back to what built it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: class Envelope(BaseModel) with data, cached_at and source.
blocks.context: how provenance reaches the dashboard rather than stopping at the pipeline

blocks.html: the record a tool writes beside whatever it produced: inputs, parameters, tool, version, and the digest of what it read. The file-level counterpart of the envelope.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the # comment lines a table carries so a figure can cite how its own numbers were sampled.
blocks.context: the standing requirement that nothing is produced without its source and generation process documented

blocks.html: the full chain from raw input to a published number: every dataset, table, feature, metric, figure and deliverable naming its sources and its transformation. Append-only, so a correction is a new record rather than an edit.
blocks.context: the repository-wide rule every artifact is held to

blocks.html: the dated line near the top of every document outside methodology/ and archive/, saying when it was last checked against reality. A document describing system state that has not been re-verified must say so.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this file's own Standing line reads 2026-10-05.
blocks.context: the freshness contract on every page in docs/

blocks.html: one numbered, append-only record of one run: the question, the inputs with versions and parameters, the exact commands, the observed output and the conclusion — enough for someone else to reproduce it. From the first research step on, an entry is a test bound to a hypothesis and carries its prediction and its refutation condition written before the run, and its verdict after.
blocks.context: the audit log of how every result was reached; entries are never edited, only superseded

blocks.html: the repository's hardest rule: never invent or assume a result. Every number, finding or conclusion comes from an actual executed run whose output is visible, and anything not run is said to be not run. It is why this dictionary quotes published schema values and arithmetic, and nothing else.
blocks.context: the rule that governs what may appear in any artifact here

blocks.html: one of the checks that must pass before Python is pushed: formatting, linting, module size, import layering, type checking, the iteration-folder check and the tests. A gate that is wrong for a change gets fixed and the reason recorded — never bypassed.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: tools/check-python.sh, with --fix to format and autofix first.
blocks.context: the pre-push contract for code in this repository

blocks.html: a fabricated test input that mirrors the awkward properties of the real file without containing any real data. A fixture can prove the machinery works and can never prove the answer is right, and tests that score against one say so in their names.
blocks.context: the testing rule for any pipeline over the challenge data

blocks.html: the app's rendering of this file, at /learn. The dictionary is generated from the markdown at build time, never copied, and the generator doubles as its link checker: a cross-link naming a missing heading, a source: naming a missing file or a related: naming an undefined term all fail the build.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: pnpm dictionary writes the generated form; pnpm dictionary:check fails on drift.
blocks.context: why the format rules at the top of this file are enforced rather than advisory
